claude.rationale: The customer-facing asset (T4) was contract drilling capacity delivered through owned/operated rig fleets, and the whole company — fleet, operations, and ~2,800 personnel — crossed the boundary together as Rowan became an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary, so no product-vs-process split is documented (gap_45=0). The deal transferred processes (T5) alongside the organization/people (T6): personnel and executive/management roles were carried over with a Rowan-designated CEO, Ensco-designated Chairman/CFO/COO/GC, and equity awards converted, showing processes and people moved together (gap_56=0). This is a share-for-share scheme combining two similarly sized firms with co-leadership drawn from both predecessors, coding T1 as imprint-share; Ensco's corporate shell survived (T3=1-1) while the two operating fleets, models, processes, and workforces combined into one (N-1).

gemini.rationale: The transaction was structured as a combination where Rowan's entire business, including its rig fleet (T4), operations (T5), and personnel (T6), transferred to Ensco as a wholly-owned subsidiary. There is no evidence in the closing structure of any mismatch or separation between the product, process, and organization.

grok.rationale: At closing the customer-facing product of both parties (contract drilling capacity delivered through each owned/operated rig fleet, including the preserved ARO interest) and the operational processes that produce it were structured to combine into one combined offshore drilling company, with no product-vs-process mismatch documented. Organization and leadership were likewise aligned at closing via a mixed board (six Ensco-designated, five Rowan-designated), a Rowan-designated CEO and Ensco-designated Executive Chairman/CFO/COO/GC, conversion of Rowan equity awards, and assumption of Rowan change-in-control agreements, so no process-vs-organization structural gap is documented.
